title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 3: The Chai Agent on Temporal
heading: Introduction
text: Written alongside our session on durable AI agents at LSEG Hyderabad on November 14. Every command here is shown for macOS / Linux and for Windows, so you can follow along on your own laptop. In part 2 the chai agent became durable. Kill it anywhere, run it again, and it carries on from the exact step and charges the customer once. But read that again: run it again. After every crash, somebody restarted it. Nothing noticed that the run had died. At 3 AM, nobody would. In this post we run the same agent on Temporal, a durable execution engine. We start two workers, kill the one that's charging the customer, and don't touch anything . The other worker finishes the order, and the customer pays once. Then we give it part 2's harder cases (a pending payment, a sold-out kitchen, a big refund) and kill the workers while it waits for people. It's free and runs on your laptop. No account is needed. Code: https://github.com/AI-Yatra/durable-ai-agents , file temporal agent.py .

title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 3: The Chai Agent on Temporal
heading: Introduction
text: There are two ways to make sure "someone" restarts a crashed agent: Examples What happens after a crash Restart the process Docker restart policy, Kubernetes, systemd The process comes back. It doesn't know which orders were half-done. You write that part. Durable execution engine Temporal, DBOS, Restate, Inngest The engine keeps the history of every run, notices a dead one, and hands it to a live worker, which carries on from the last finished step. We'll use Temporal. The ideas carry over to the others.

title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 3: The Chai Agent on Temporal
heading: Four words of Temporal
text: - Workflow: the agent loop. It's ordinary code that says what happens in what order. Temporal records each step it takes. - Activity: one step that touches the outside world: the LLM call, the charge, the SMS, the kitchen. Activities can fail and be retried. - Worker: a process that runs your workflows and activities. You can run as many as you like, and any of them can pick up any run. - Server: keeps the event history of every workflow ("read order finished with this result, charge upi started…"), and hands work to workers. The event history plays the role the SQLite checkpoints played in part 2. The difference is that the server watches it.

title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 3: The Chai Agent on Temporal
heading: How Temporal notices a dead worker
text: While charge upi runs, it calls activity.heartbeat() every second. When a kill -9 stops the heartbeats, the server waits 3 seconds, marks that attempt as failed, and schedules a retry, which any live worker can pick up.

title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 3: The Chai Agent on Temporal
heading: The workflow: the agent loop
text: The happy path is the first four lines, and it reads like the normal agent from part 1. The rest is part 2's branches, written as plain if and while instead of graph edges. There's one rule for workflow code: it must be deterministic. When a worker picks up a run, it replays the workflow function from the top, and each execute activity that already finished returns its recorded result from the history instead of running again. That's how read order (and its LLM call) is never repeated. So no random numbers, clocks, network calls or environment variables directly in the workflow: those belong in activities. That's why the refund limit and the customer's timeout come in with the order ( job ) instead of being read from os.environ inside run . And the idempotency key is built from the workflow id, which is the same on every replay. title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 3: The Chai Agent on Temporal
heading: Waiting for people
text: Part 2's agent paused for the bank, the customer and an admin with interrupt() , and somebody ran the script again with the answer. On Temporal, a wait is two small pieces of the workflow class: A signal is a message sent to a running workflow, and Temporal writes it into the history like everything else. wait condition pauses the workflow until the answer is there. While it waits, no worker is busy and no process has to stay up: the wait lives on the server. A @workflow.query called waiting lets the command line ask "who are you waiting for?" before it answers. The timeout is a durable timer : the server keeps the clock. If the customer never replies, the order refunds itself after CUSTOMER TIMEOUT seconds (default 2 hours), even if every worker was restarted in between. In part 2, someone had to run customer no-reply .

title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 1: Build a Chai Agent, Then Kill It
heading: Introduction
text: Written alongside our session on durable AI agents at LSEG Hyderabad on November 14. Every command here is shown for macOS / Linux and for Windows, so you can follow along on your own laptop. A customer sends a message: "4 chai for 98765 43210" . An agent reads it, charges ₹80 over UPI, texts a receipt and tells the kitchen to make four chai. That's the whole agent. It works. Then the process dies one second after the charge, and when it comes back the customer pays again. This series is about that second. In this post we build the agent and break it. title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 1: Build a Chai Agent, Then Kill It
heading: Why
text: Everything the agent knew lived in RAM: the parsed order, the fact that charge upi had finished, the receipt. kill -9 threw all of it away. The new process had no idea an earlier one existed, so it did the only thing it could, which was to start from the top. Starting from the top is fine for a step like read order , which only costs money and time. It's not fine for charge upi , because that step changed something in someone else's system, and that change didn't die with our process. That's the difference between two kinds of steps: Step Run it twice and… read order (LLM) you pay for tokens twice. Annoying. charge upi (bank) the customer pays twice. A support ticket, a refund and a lost customer. send receipt (SMS) the customer gets two texts. Confusing. send to kitchen four extra chai nobody paid for.

title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 1: Build a Chai Agent, Then Kill It
heading: Introduction
text: Most agent harnesses (coding agents, chat frameworks) do save the chat history: you can close the window and pick the conversation up again. That's persistence . It saves what was said . What we need is durability : saving what was done , step by step, so that after a crash the agent continues from the exact step instead of starting over, and never repeats something the world already saw. A saved conversation that ends with "I'll charge the customer now" doesn't tell you whether the charge happened.

title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 1: Build a Chai Agent, Then Kill It
heading: What a durable agent has to promise
text: 1. Resume from the exact step. After a crash, continue where it stopped, not from the top. 2. Side effects happen once. A charge that went through is never sent again. 3. Wait for a person. Some steps need a human (a bank confirming, a customer choosing, an admin approving), and that wait can take hours. The wait has to survive restarts too. 4. Write every step down. When the customer calls asking "where's my money?" , you can answer. In part 2 we add all four to this agent, in one file. The kill test stays the same, and the result changes: payments made: 1 .

title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 2: Make the Chai Agent Survive kill -9
heading: Fix 1: save every step to disk
text: The normal agent saved its state after every step, to memory: The durable one saves it to a SQLite file: There's one more setting, and it's the one people miss: LangGraph's default is "async" : the checkpoint is written in the background while the next step already runs . That's faster, and a kill -9 at the wrong moment loses the last step. "sync" writes each checkpoint to disk before the next step starts. For steps that touch money, that's the one you want. Now, when the agent starts, it can ask whether there's a saved run for this order: The thread id in the config ( order-1 ) is the key to all of this. One order, one thread, one saved history.

title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 2: Make the Chai Agent Survive kill -9
heading: Is that enough?
text: Suppose we stopped here, with checkpoints but nothing else. Kill it after the charge, the same as in part 1, and the second run looks like this (shortened; the repo's durable agent.py already has the next fix, so you'll see this only if you take fix 2 out): There's good news and bad news: - Good: no LLM call line. read order finished before the crash, its result was on disk, and it came back for free. - Bad: it still charged twice . The reason: a checkpoint is saved after a step finishes. charge upi was killed halfway, after the bank charged but before the step returned, so as far as LangGraph knows it never ran. On resume it runs again, and the bank sees what looks like a brand-new payment. This is true of every durable system, Temporal included: a step that dies in the middle runs again. That's called at-least-once . You can't checkpoint your way out of it, because there will always be a gap between "the bank did it" and "we wrote it down". What you can do is make running it again harmless.

title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 2: Make the Chai Agent Survive kill -9
heading: Fix 2: charge once, with an idempotency key
text: An idempotency key is a unique id you send with a request. The bank remembers it: if the same key comes in twice, it returns the original result instead of charging again. Many payment APIs support this; Stripe's Idempotency-Key header is the best-known example. The trick is where you make the key . It has to be made once , and saved before the charge: Because read order finished and was checkpointed, the key is on disk. When charge upi re-runs, it sends the same key. title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 2: Make the Chai Agent Survive kill -9
heading: Introduction
text: Fixes 1 and 2 cover the clean crash. Real life is messier. Here's the case we'll handle: The customer pays. The agent crashes. Two minutes later it's back, and two things have changed: 1. The payment is pending : the money left the customer's account but hasn't reached the shop. (Anyone who has used UPI has seen this. The bank settles it later: success, or reversed.) 2. The chai is sold out . What should the agent do? - Retry the charge? No. That's a second payment. - Refund? Not yet. If you refund now and the bank later reverses the pending payment, the customer gets ₹160 back for an ₹80 order. A refund can't be undone, so never refund money you don't have yet. - Wait for the bank. Yes. Then, once the money is really ours, ask the customer what they want. The tricky part is that the wait can take minutes, hours, or until the next day. You can't hold a process open that long, and if you do, it will crash. The wait has to be saved , like every other step. LangGraph's tool for this is interrupt() . It pauses the graph, saves the pause in the checkpoint, and returns control to you. title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 2: Make the Chai Agent Survive kill -9
heading: Fix 4: write every step down
text: When the customer calls on Monday asking "where's my money?" , or the auditor asks "who approved this refund?" , you need an answer. You already have one. With a checkpointer, LangGraph keeps every checkpoint, not just the last. The history of a thread is an audit log: Each step has a time, what changed, and how long each wait took. In real life those waits are hours, not seconds. One warning: LangGraph can also replay from an old checkpoint ("time travel"). Replaying re-runs every later step for real, so without the idempotency keys from fix 2, that's a great way to refund twice.

title: Building Durable AI Agents, Part 2: Make the Chai Agent Survive kill -9
heading: Introduction
text: Look at what we did after every crash: we restarted it by hand. A checkpoint saves the work, but nothing notices that the run died. If the process dies at 3 AM, the order sits half-done until someone comes in at 10. If two people restart it, two processes run the same order. You could add a restart policy ( restart: unless-stopped , Kubernetes, systemd). The process would come back, but it wouldn't know which orders were half-done. You'd still write the "find stalled runs and resume them" code yourself, along with the locking that stops two processes grabbing the same order. That's exactly what a durable execution engine does. In part 3 we run the same chai agent on Temporal: kill the worker, type nothing, and watch the order finish anyway.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: AI Operating System (AI OS): Is This the Future of Computing?
text: From opening applications and clicking buttons to simply telling computers what we want. Discover how Artificial Intelligence is changing the way we interact with technology. Imagine starting your day by telling your computer: "Check my emails, summarize the important ones, prepare a presentation for today's meeting, collect the latest market updates, and share everything with my team." Your computer understands the request, breaks it into smaller tasks, uses different applications, gathers information, prepares the presentation, and brings everything together. You don't have to open ten different applications or manually perform every step. This is the idea behind an AI Operating System (AI OS) . Artificial Intelligence is no longer limited to answering questions or generating text. It is gradually moving towards systems that can understand instructions, plan tasks, interact with applications, and perform actions independently. But what exactly is an AI OS? How is it different from Windows or macOS? Are there any real examples today? And what could it mean for the future of work? Let's explore. ---

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: From Traditional Computing to Intelligent Computing
text: To understand why AI OS matters, let's first look at how we currently interact with computers. Think about a normal working day. You open your browser to search for information, Excel to analyze data, Outlook to check emails, Teams to attend meetings, and other applications to complete your work. Every application performs a specific function, but you are responsible for connecting all the steps. This is how traditional computing works: the user operates the applications to achieve an outcome. An AI-powered approach changes this interaction. Instead of navigating through different applications, you describe the outcome you want, and an intelligent system coordinates the required actions. The shift is from manually operating individual applications to describing an outcome and letting connected tools work together.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: What Exactly Is an AI Operating System?
text: An Operating System (OS) is the fundamental software that manages a computer's hardware, software, memory, processes, and applications. Some familiar examples are Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS. An AI Operating System takes this concept further by introducing an intelligent layer that understands user intent, manages context, coordinates AI agents, and connects different tools and applications to complete tasks. In simple words: A traditional OS helps you operate your computer. An AI OS aims to help your computer understand what you want to accomplish and work towards completing it. It is important to understand that AI OS is an evolving concept, not one universally defined product or a completely new replacement for Windows and Linux. Some implementations integrate AI into existing operating systems, while others build dedicated platforms for running and coordinating AI agents.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: How Is an AI OS Different From a Traditional OS?
text: The biggest difference is how users interact with technology. Traditional OS AI OS Application-driven Intent-driven Users manually open applications AI can select and use tools Executes predefined instructions Can interpret and plan tasks Limited understanding of context Can use context and memory Users connect individual workflows Agents can coordinate workflows Focuses on managing computing resources Also coordinates intelligent tasks Consider this example. You want to organize a business meeting. With a traditional OS, you open your calendar, check availability, open email, draft invitations, and prepare an agenda. With an AI OS, you could simply say: "Schedule a meeting with the engineering team next week, find a suitable time, prepare an agenda, and send invitations." The AI system can coordinate the necessary applications and services to accomplish the task, with your permission. The difference is not simply speed. It is a change in how we communicate with computers.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: What Happens Inside an AI OS?
text: An AI OS is not just one large language model or a chatbot running in the background. It brings together several technologies that work as a coordinated system. Here are some of its important building blocks: Component Its role Large Language Models (LLMs) Understand instructions, interpret context, and reason about tasks AI Agents Perform specialized tasks such as research, coding, and analysis Memory & Context Retain useful information and previous interactions Orchestration Engine Coordinates agents and manages task execution APIs & Tool Integrations Connect with external applications, databases, and services Security & Permissions Controls what agents can access and which actions they can perform

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: Understanding the workflow through an example
text: Imagine asking your AI OS to prepare a report on the latest developments in Artificial Intelligence. Instead of doing everything yourself, the system can follow a workflow: The process can be explained through a few simple steps: - Understanding: The AI interprets what you are asking for. - Planning: It divides the request into smaller tasks. - Delegation: It assigns tasks to specialized agents. - Execution: Agents use permitted tools, APIs, and data sources. - Verification: The system checks whether the requested tasks were completed correctly. - Delivery: The final output is presented to the user. For example, a research agent can collect information, an analysis agent can identify important findings, and a writing agent can prepare the report. The orchestration layer coordinates their work. This is what makes an AI OS more interesting than an ordinary chatbot.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: AI Chatbots, AI Agents and AI OS: What Is the Difference?
text: These three terms are often used interchangeably, but they represent different capabilities. Capability AI Chatbot AI Agent AI OS Answers questions Yes Yes Yes Understands instructions Yes Yes Yes Performs actions Tool-dependent Yes Coordinates actions Uses external applications Sometimes Yes Across connected systems Handles multi-step tasks Limited Yes Yes Coordinates multiple agents Usually not Not necessarily A central capability Manages shared context and permissions Application-dependent Application-dependent A broader system-level responsibility Think of an AI chatbot as someone who answers your questions. An AI agent is someone who can take responsibility for a task. An AI OS is the environment that brings multiple agents, tools, memory, and applications together to accomplish larger goals.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: Are AI Operating Systems Already Here?
text: Yes, but there is an important distinction. We already have products and research projects moving towards AI-native and agent-based computing. However, they do not all represent the same thing. Some are AI-enhanced operating systems, some are dedicated agentic operating systems, and others are enterprise platforms. Here are some interesting examples.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: rabbit OS 3 – An Agentic Operating System
text: rabbit OS 3, announced in September 2026, is an interesting example of the agentic OS direction. Rather than requiring users to operate individual applications for every task, rabbit OS 3 provides a conversational interface where users describe the outcome they want. It can coordinate connected AI models, web services, skills, and devices. Its desktop experience can also interact with Windows, macOS, and Linux devices through a connected agent. The central idea is simple: tell the system what you want to accomplish, rather than manually managing every step.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: Android with Gemini Intelligence
text: Google is also moving Android towards a more intelligent operating experience. With Gemini Intelligence, announced in May 2026, Google is bringing more proactive AI capabilities to Android, including automating multi-step tasks across applications. Android is not being replaced by a separate AI OS here. Instead, intelligence is becoming a deeper part of the existing operating system.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: Windows Copilot+ PCs
text: Microsoft is integrating AI directly into Windows through Copilot+ PCs. These devices include dedicated AI components and hardware, such as Neural Processing Units (NPUs), to run certain AI workloads locally. This enables features such as AI-assisted image creation, editing, and language processing. It is an example of an existing operating system becoming more AI-powered rather than a completely new AI OS.

text: Another interesting example is AIOS by AGI Research. Unlike consumer operating systems, this project focuses on building an operating system specifically for LLM-based agents. It introduces an AIOS kernel that manages important resources such as: - Agent scheduling - Memory management - Context management - Storage management - Access control - LLM and tool resources The objective is to provide a structured environment where multiple AI agents can run and interact more efficiently. This is particularly interesting from a software engineering and AI research perspective.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: Interesting Facts: What Makes AI OS Different?
text: A few ideas from operating-systems research become especially interesting when applied to AI agents: - Agents need scheduling too. If several agents request access to a model or tool at the same time, a system needs a way to manage and prioritize those requests. - Context is a resource. Agents rely on context windows, memory, and relevant task history. Managing what information each agent receives can affect both cost and quality. - Tool access is a security boundary. An agent that can read a document should not automatically be allowed to delete it, send it externally, or approve a transaction. - Local AI changes the architecture. Devices with Neural Processing Units (NPUs) can accelerate supported AI workloads on-device, while larger or more demanding tasks may still use cloud models. - An AI OS needs more than a powerful model. Scheduling, memory, tool integration, observability, permissions, and recovery from errors are all part of making agent systems dependable. title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: Beyond the Basics: What Would Make an AI OS a Real Operating System?
text: It is easy to imagine an AI OS as a chatbot connected to a collection of tools. But that alone is not enough. A dependable AI OS needs a runtime: a layer that manages how tasks are created, scheduled, executed, monitored, paused, resumed, and completed. This is where ideas from traditional operating-system design become useful. Think of an AI agent as a process. It has a goal, a current state, a context, resource requirements, and a set of permissions. The AI OS is responsible for coordinating those processes safely.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: The lifecycle of an AI task
text: A useful way to understand this is to follow a task from the moment a user makes a request until the result is delivered. The important detail is that the system does not simply ask an LLM to do everything. It separates planning, authorization, execution, and verification.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: The OS concepts behind an AI OS
text: Traditional OS concept AI OS equivalent Why it matters Process scheduling Agent and task scheduling Decides which agent runs and when Memory management Context and agent memory management Controls what information is available to each task File system Persistent task state and knowledge storage Allows work to be saved and resumed Permissions and users Tool scopes and agent identities Limits what an agent is allowed to do Inter-process communication Agent-to-agent messages and shared task state Enables collaboration without losing context Monitoring and logging Traces, token usage, tool logs, and task status Makes failures and costs visible Error handling Retries, timeouts, fallback models, and recovery Prevents one failed tool call from breaking the whole workflow This comparison is an architectural analogy, not a claim that every AI OS implements these features exactly like a conventional operating system.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: Why orchestration matters more than simply adding more agents
text: Imagine a task that requires three agents: - A research agent gathers information. - An analysis agent checks the findings. - A writing agent prepares the final report. If these agents run without coordination, they may repeat work, use outdated information, or disagree about which result is correct. An orchestration layer can define dependencies, pass structured outputs between agents, enforce timeouts, and decide when a task is ready for review. For example: This is a simple sequential workflow. More advanced systems can run independent tasks in parallel and combine their results later.

The following simplified example shows how an orchestration layer can check permissions before allowing an action. It is illustrative application code, not a production security system. Here, the agent can search the web and read documents, but it cannot automatically send emails, delete files, or access financial systems. A production implementation would also need authenticated identities, server-side authorization, audit logs, input validation, isolation, and approval checks. A prompt instruction alone is not a security boundary.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: The difficult engineering questions
text: Building an AI OS introduces questions that ordinary application development does not always face: - How should tasks be scheduled? Should urgent tasks run first? How do we prevent one agent from consuming all available model capacity? - How should memory be shared? What should be private to one agent, and what can be shared across a team of agents? - How do we prevent loops? An agent might repeatedly call tools without making progress. Systems need step limits, timeouts, and budgets. - How do we measure success? A model response is not proof that an action was completed. The system needs to verify the actual result. - How do we recover? If a network request fails halfway through a workflow, the system should know what succeeded and what can safely be retried. These are the problems that turn an impressive AI demo into dependable infrastructure.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: A New Design Principle: Human Intent, Machine Execution, Human Accountability
text: The most useful AI OS may not be the one that automates everything. It may be the one that knows when to act independently and when to ask. A sensible system can handle low-risk tasks, such as summarizing documents or organizing information, while asking for confirmation before sending external messages, changing permissions, deleting data, or initiating financial actions. This creates a practical division of responsibility: Work type Suitable system behavior Low-risk, reversible tasks Automate with clear activity logs Tasks affecting other people Prepare the action and request confirmation Sensitive or financial actions Require explicit authorization and stronger checks High-impact decisions Provide evidence and recommendations; keep a human accountable This is a key part of making AI-native computing trustworthy. The goal is not to remove people from every workflow, but to reduce repetitive coordination while preserving human control.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: AI OS in the Workplace: The Next Big Shift
text: One of the most exciting applications of AI OS is not necessarily on personal computers. It is in the workplace. Think about a modern organization. Employees use dozens of applications for communication, customer management, financial analysis, project management, reporting, and development. Information is distributed across multiple systems, and employees spend a significant amount of time moving between them. An AI-powered work environment could bring these systems together through intelligent agents. Imagine an employee asking: "Give me a summary of this week's project progress, identify delayed tasks, check the latest customer updates, and prepare a management report." A coordinated AI environment could involve: Specialized Agent What it does Email Agent Summarizes important communication Project Agent Checks project progress and pending tasks Data Agent Collects and analyzes business data Research Agent Finds relevant external information Reporting Agent Prepares the management report Coordinator Connects the results and manages the workflow Instead of manually collecting information from different systems, employees could interact with a unified intelligent interface.

However, they demonstrate how enterprise software is evolving towards connected, intelligent, and agent-driven operations.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: What Could the Future of AI OS Look Like?
text: The future of computing could look very different from what we are familiar with today. We may gradually move through the following stages: Traditional Computing Users manually operate applications and manage individual tasks. AI-Assisted Computing AI assistants help users write, search, summarize, and generate content. Agentic Computing AI agents can plan, use tools, collaborate, and execute multi-step tasks. AI-Native Computing AI becomes deeply integrated into the operating environment, with persistent context, coordinated agents, and intelligent automation. The Future of Work A unified intelligent environment could coordinate applications, employees, data, and specialized AI agents across an organization. This does not mean traditional operating systems will disappear overnight. Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, and iOS will likely continue to provide the underlying infrastructure. The bigger change could be the intelligent layer built on top of them.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: What Are the Challenges?
text: Despite the possibilities, building a reliable AI OS comes with significant challenges. Privacy and Data Protection: AI systems may need access to emails, documents, business information, and personal data. This information must be protected. Security and Permissions: An AI agent should not have unrestricted access to every application or system. Access must be controlled. Accuracy and Reliability: AI systems can misunderstand instructions or produce incorrect results. Important actions need verification. Human Oversight: Financial transactions, sensitive communications, and critical business decisions may require human approval. Integration: Connecting different applications, databases, and services reliably is a complex engineering challenge. The goal should not simply be to build an AI system that can do everything. It should be to build one that can do useful things safely, accurately, and transparently.

title: AI Operating System (AI OS): The Next Evolution of How We Use Computers
heading: The Bigger Picture
text: The evolution of computing has always been about making technology easier to use. We moved from command-line interfaces to graphical interfaces, from standalone applications to cloud platforms, and now towards AI-powered assistants and agents. AI Operating Systems represent another possible evolution. Instead of learning how to operate every application, users may increasingly describe the outcomes they want and allow intelligent systems to coordinate the work. For businesses, this could mean more connected workflows and less manual coordination. For individuals, it could mean a more personalised and intelligent computing experience. We are still in the early stages, and many technical and security challenges remain. But one thing is becoming clear: the future of computing may not be defined by how many applications we can use, but by how intelligently those applications can work together. Perhaps the next big evolution in computing is not another application or another operating system. It is a system that understands our intentions and helps turn them into reality. --- Further reading and references: - rabbit OS 3 – Official announcement - Google – Gemini Intelligence on Android

text: Figure 2. Overview of the Memorilla architecture. Snowflakes mark frozen components and the flame marks the trained one. Memorilla delivers its fixed budget by separating storage, recall, and generation into three components, and only the middle one is trained. Store. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B encoder turns each chunk into one mean-pooled vector of 2,560 values. A 200-chat history becomes a 200 x 2,560 matrix of about 1 MB. title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: Introduction
text: A cactus is approaching. The dinosaur has three choices: keep running, jump, or duck. Make the wrong choice at the wrong moment and the run ends. Tiny Dino, a project published by GitHub user syedazeez337, turns that familiar game into a compact machine-learning experiment. Its shipped policy has just 21,699 parameters . The repository reports that this checkpoint completed 1,000,000 simulated frames without a crash , with no runtime planner correcting its actions. The useful story is how the project connects a small model to a precise input contract, an offline teacher, and several checks on the exact artifact being deployed. Reading the code also reveals boundaries that matter when interpreting those results.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: What the network actually sees
text: This policy does not watch screenshots. It receives a 28-value structured state vector extracted directly from the simulation. Those features describe the game speed, the dinosaur’s vertical position and velocity, its movement and control state, and the two nearest obstacles. Obstacle features include relative distance, width, height, vertical position, and type. Missing-obstacle indicators distinguish an absent obstacle from an obstacle whose numeric features happen to be zero. The distinction matters. Recognizing a cactus in an image and choosing when to jump are separate problems. Tiny Dino focuses on choosing actions once the relevant state is available. Its engine advances at a fixed 60 frames per second and reimplements Chromium-related physics and collision semantics. Courses are seeded, making runs repeatable within this implementation. This is a controlled simulator rather than a screen-reading agent operating an arbitrary browser game.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: A small network with a clear job
text: Architecture at a glance. The teacher supplies supervision offline; the deployed policy chooses each action directly. Diagram based on the repository implementation. The deployed architecture is a feed-forward multilayer perceptron with three hidden layers, each 96 units wide, SiLU activations, and three output scores. Its dimensions are: 28 inputs → 96 → 96 → 96 → 3 action scores Including biases, that is 21,699 trainable parameters. The shipped FP32 checkpoint occupies 90,929 bytes; that file includes metadata as well as weights. At each frame, the runtime extracts and normalizes the state, runs the network, computes action probabilities, and selects the largest probability. It applies that action directly to the engine. There is no teacher consulted during live play and no fallback rule that replaces a risky prediction. The runtime validates inputs, output shape, and finite values, but those checks do not choose a safer action. The model remains responsible for the gameplay decision. The probability display in the web app helps readers inspect the model’s preferences. It should not be interpreted as a calibrated probability of surviving the next obstacle.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: A timing intuition
text: Imagine the same cactus at the same distance in two runs, with the game moving faster in the second. The dinosaur has less time to react in that faster run. If it is already falling from a jump, the useful action may change again. That is why the inputs include speed and motion, as well as obstacle distance.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: An offline teacher supplies the examples
text: A tiny policy can be cheap at inference because more work happens before deployment. Tiny Dino’s teacher evaluates the three candidate first actions by forward simulation. After that first step it follows a deterministic continuation policy, looking ahead for a bounded number of frames or until the target obstacle is passed. Certification uses a 90-frame horizon. This is narrower than searching every possible future action sequence. A teacher-approved action survives the particular bounded rollout used by the checker; it is not a guarantee of indefinite survival. The corpus generator uses these verdicts to choose labels. It prefers the teacher’s continuation action when acceptable and otherwise picks an acceptable alternative. The training command also adds offline expert trajectories from a separate seed group and repeats boundary examples to emphasize timing-sensitive cases. The repository contains a DAgger-style collector for states visited by a learned policy. However, the exposed training command currently adds teacher-controlled expert rollouts. These are distinct data-collection paths, and the code does not establish that the shipped checkpoint came from a full iterative DAg

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: What the recorded results show
text: Different checks answer different questions. These figures summarize committed repository records, not a fresh benchmark. The following numbers come from the repository’s committed evidence and deployment records. They are reported results, not measurements independently rerun for this article. Check Recorded result Deployed model 21,699 parameters, FP32 Checkpoint file 90,929 bytes Frozen certification grid 5,400 states checked Choices rejected by the bounded teacher 0 Certification cases excluded for no acceptable action 0 Held-out and soak evaluation 20 seeds, 50,000 frames each Total simulated frames 1,000,000 Recorded crashes 0 Runtime action interventions 0 Reported CPU latency 0.0484 ms p50; 0.0545 ms p95; 0.0709 ms p99 The certification grid varies speeds, obstacle distances, obstacle types and bird heights, control ages, and selected paired-obstacle gaps. It deliberately samples distances densely around timing boundaries. Those latency figures should stay attached to their recorded benchmark. They do not measure browser rendering, HTTP round trips, or an end-to-end user interaction, and they are not a promise for every machine.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: Why certification and long runs answer different questions
text: The certification checker asks whether each selected action belongs to the teacher’s acceptable set on a fixed grid. Long runs ask whether sequences of the model’s own decisions keep the game alive. There is an additional detail in the implementation: the corpus generator uses the same synthetic scenario grid as certification. Changing the seed field does not turn these synthetic states into unseen feature combinations. Passing this grid is therefore a finite conformance check, not an independent held-out generalization benchmark. The trajectory tests provide complementary evidence, but they also remain finite: seeds 201 through 220, with a fixed maximum length per run. They do not cover every possible course, state, physics variation, or future frame. The project records a useful failure. A GPU-trained candidate passed certification but failed its soak evaluation, so it was rejected. The README also describes a retrained model crashing on seed 202 at frame 2,327 after passing certification. That is why a successful retraining run cannot simply inherit the shipped model’s results. The new weights need their own checks.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: Two optimizations that did not earn deployment
text: The repository’s INT8 experiment reduced the candidate artifact to 29,049 bytes, but changed 36 of the 5,400 certification actions . It failed the project’s exact action-parity criterion, so the FP32 model was retained. Changed actions are not automatically unsafe actions. The recorded experiment establishes a parity failure; it does not demonstrate that all 36 changes caused collisions. The practical lesson is to re-evaluate behavior after compression before promoting a new artifact. The GPU training record needs similar care. It reports a training duration of about 16.48 seconds on an RTX 3050 laptop GPU, but identifies a candidate that was rejected. That duration should not be advertised as the verified training time of the deployed checkpoint or the complete data-generation-and-training workflow.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: Keeping the evidence attached to the weights
text: One of the strongest engineering details is the checkpoint evidence chain. The runtime checks the checkpoint schema, engine revision, feature version, and feature-layout hash before loading the model. This reduces the risk of silently feeding weights a different interpretation of the inputs. An end-to-end test then ties the checkpoint’s SHA-256 hash to the certification, evidence summary, and soak records. Its purpose is straightforward: establish that the model being served is the model named in those records. A passing report for yesterday’s weights should not become evidence for today’s replacement file.

heading: Introduction
text: EmbeddingGemma 2 is Google’s latest open embedding model for semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Built on Gemma 4, it maps text, source code, images, video, and audio into a shared 768-dimensional vector space. It is released under the Apache 2.0 license and scales from 270 million to 740 million parameters depending on the modalities you enable.

title: EmbeddingGemma 2: A Compact Multimodal Embedding Model
heading: Why EmbeddingGemma 2 matters?
text: Traditional multimodal search systems often require separate models for text, images, audio, and video. EmbeddingGemma 2 provides a unified alternative: Search source code using natural-language queries. Find images using text descriptions. Search audio recordings and video clips semantically. Build multimodal RAG pipelines. Run local or on-device retrieval with a relatively small model. Store embeddings in a single compatible vector space. For example, a query such as “waterproof trail shoes” can be compared with text, product images, or a video showing the shoes being tested on wet rocks.

text: One of the most useful improvements is its code-understanding capability. Google reports that EmbeddingGemma 2 performs 14% better than EmbeddingGemma 1 on the MTEB Code benchmark. This makes it suitable for: Searching large GitHub repositories. Finding relevant functions from natural-language questions. Building coding assistants. Indexing technical documentation and source code. Supporting agentic code-search workflows. A developer could ask: “Where is authentication token refresh implemented?” The embedding model can retrieve the most relevant files, classes, or functions before an LLM generates the final answer.

title: EmbeddingGemma 2: A Compact Multimodal Embedding Model
heading: Matryoshka Representation Learning
text: EmbeddingGemma 2 supports Matryoshka Representation Learning, or MRL. This allows the original 768-dimensional vector to be truncated to a smaller size while preserving much of its semantic quality. Dimensions Recommended use 768 or 512 Highest recall and multimodal retrieval 256 Storage-constrained indexes 128 Large text-only indexes and first-stage shortlisting At 256 dimensions, the model retains most of its quality for text and code and approximately 95% of its retrieval quality for image, video, and speech. At 128 dimensions, text and code retain around 90% quality, while multimodal retrieval quality can fall to approximately 75%. These figures should be validated against your own data before deployment. Reducing the vector size can significantly lower storage requirements. For example, one million 768-dimensional vectors require roughly 1.5 GB in bfloat16, while 128-dimensional vectors require approximately 250 MB.

title: Speculative Decoding — 2-3x Faster Inference in 60 Lines of PyTorch
heading: What we covered
text: Autoregressive decoding is slow because it generates one token per forward pass. Speculative decoding breaks that bottleneck — with zero change in outputs. - Draft-verify-accept — a small draft model proposes tokens, the big model verifies them in parallel. Accept the matches, keep the guarantees. - Why it is lossless — the acceptance criterion provably preserves the target distribution. Speed without sampling drift. - HF assisted generation + llama.cpp — the same idea in production tooling, configured and benchmarked live.

heading: What we built

title: Speculative Decoding — 2-3x Faster Inference in 60 Lines of PyTorch
heading: Takeaways
text: - The fastest token is the one you don't recompute — verification parallelizes, drafting is cheap. - Lossless matters: speculation is an exact optimization, not an approximation. - 64 people, one lab, every laptop showing the same speedup. That is the AIYatra format.
